paragraphs: The tendency of the principle of legislation for States, or communities, in their political capacities has been shown by the experiment we have made of it. It is equally shown by the fate of all other governments of the confederate kind of which we have any account, in exact proportion to how far the principle prevailed in those systems. The confirmations of this fact deserve a separate and particular examination. For now I shall content myself with merely observing that, of all the confederacies of antiquity that history has handed down to us, the Lycian and Achaean leagues, as far as traces of them remain, appear to have been the most free from the fetters of this mistaken principle. They were accordingly the ones that have best deserved, and most liberally received, the applauding judgment of political writers.

This objectionable principle may, as truly as emphatically, be called the parent of anarchy. It has been seen that delinquencies in the members of the Union are its natural and necessary offspring, and that whenever they occur the only constitutional remedy is force, and the immediate effect of using it is civil war.

It remains to inquire how far so odious an engine of government, as applied to us, would even be capable of achieving its end. If there were not a large army constantly at the disposal of the national government, it would either be unable to use force at all or, when it could be used, it would amount to a war between parts of the Confederacy over the infractions of a league. In such a war the strongest combination would be the most likely to prevail, whether it consisted of those who supported or of those who resisted the general authority. It would rarely happen that the delinquency to be redressed was confined to a single member, and if more than one had neglected their duty, the similarity of their situation would lead them to unite for common defense. Apart from this motive of sympathy, if a large and influential State should happen to be the offending member, it would commonly have weight enough with its neighbors to win some of them over as allies to its cause. Specious arguments of danger to the common liberty could easily be contrived, and plausible excuses for the party's failures could without difficulty be invented. These would alarm the fears, inflame the passions, and win the good will even of States not chargeable with any violation or omission of duty. This would be the more likely to happen because the delinquencies of the larger members might sometimes be expected to proceed from the ambitious calculation of their rulers, who wished to rid themselves of all outside control over their designs of personal aggrandizement. To carry this out better, it is to be presumed they would first tamper with leading individuals in the neighboring States. If allies could not be found at home, recourse would be had to foreign powers, who would seldom be reluctant to encourage the dissensions of a Confederacy whose firm union they had so much reason to fear. Once the sword is drawn, the passions of men observe no bounds of moderation. The promptings of wounded pride and the instigations of irritated resentment would tend to carry the States against which the arms of the Union were used to any extreme necessary to avenge the affront or to avoid the disgrace of submission. The first war of this kind would probably end in the dissolution of the Union.

This may be considered the violent death of the Confederacy. Its more natural death is the one we now seem about to experience, if the federal system is not speedily renewed in a more substantial form. Considering the character of this country, it is not probable that the complying States would often be inclined to support the authority of the Union by making war on the non-complying States. They would always be readier to take the milder course of putting themselves on an equal footing with the delinquent members by imitating their example. And so the guilt of all would become the security of all. Our past experience has shown this spirit at work in its full light. There would in fact be an insuperable difficulty in determining when force could properly be used. In the matter of money contributions, which would be the most usual source of delinquency, it would often be impossible to decide whether the failure had come from unwillingness or from inability. The pretense of the latter would always be at hand. And the case would have to be very flagrant for its falseness to be detected with enough certainty to justify the harsh expedient of compulsion. It is easy to see that this problem alone, every time it occurred, would open a wide field for the exercise of factional views, of bias, and of oppression in whatever majority happened to prevail in the national council.

It seems to require no pains to prove that the States ought not to prefer a national Constitution that could be kept in motion only by a large army continually on foot to carry out the ordinary requisitions or decrees of the government. And yet this is the plain alternative involved for those who wish to deny it the power of extending its operations to individuals. Such a scheme, if practicable at all, would instantly degenerate into a military despotism; but it will be found impracticable in every light. The resources of the Union would not be equal to the upkeep of an army large enough to keep the larger States within the limits of their duty, nor would the means ever be furnished to form such an army in the first place. Whoever considers the population and strength of several of these States singly at the present time, and looks ahead to what they will become even half a century from now, will at once dismiss as idle and visionary any scheme that aims at regulating their movements by laws to operate on them in their collective capacities, and to be executed by a coercion applicable to them in the same capacities. A project of this kind is little less romantic than the monster-taming spirit attributed to the fabulous heroes and demigods of antiquity.

Even in those confederacies composed of members smaller than many of our counties, the principle of legislation for sovereign States, supported by military coercion, has never been found effective. It has rarely been attempted except against the weaker members, and in most instances attempts to coerce the refractory and disobedient have been the signal for bloody wars in which one half of the confederacy has raised its banners against the other half.

The result of these observations, to an intelligent mind, must clearly be this. If it is possible at all to construct a federal government capable of regulating the common concerns and preserving the general tranquillity, it must be founded, as to the objects committed to its care, on the reverse of the principle contended for by the opponents of the proposed Constitution. It must carry its agency to the persons of the citizens. It must need no intermediate legislations, but must itself be empowered to employ the arm of the ordinary public official to carry out its own resolutions. The majesty of the national authority must be shown through the medium of the courts of justice. The government of the Union, like that of each State, must be able to address itself directly to the hopes and fears of individuals, and to draw to its support those passions which have the strongest influence on the human heart. It must, in short, possess all the means, and have a right to resort to all the methods, of executing the powers entrusted to it that are possessed and used by the governments of the particular States.

To this reasoning it may perhaps be objected that if any State were disaffected toward the authority of the Union, it could at any time obstruct the execution of its laws and bring the matter to the same issue of force, the necessity of which is held against the opposite scheme.

The plausibility of this objection vanishes the moment we notice the essential difference between mere NON-COMPLIANCE and DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE. If the intervention of the State legislatures is needed to give effect to a measure of the Union, they have only NOT TO ACT, or TO ACT EVASIVELY, and the measure is defeated. This neglect of duty may be disguised under affected but insubstantial provisions, so as not to appear, and so not to alarm the people for the safety of the Constitution. The State leaders may even take credit for their sly invasions of it, on the ground of some temporary convenience, exemption, or advantage.

But if the execution of the laws of the national government did not require the intervention of the State legislatures, and they were to take effect directly on the citizens themselves, the particular governments could not interrupt their progress without an open and violent exercise of unconstitutional power. No omissions or evasions would serve the purpose. The States would be obliged to act, and in such a manner as to leave no doubt that they had encroached on the national rights. An experiment of this kind would always be hazardous in the face of a constitution in any degree capable of defending itself, and of a people enlightened enough to distinguish between a legal exercise and an illegal usurpation of authority. To succeed it would require not merely a factional majority in the legislature but the concurrence of the courts of justice and of the body of the people. If the judges were not part of a conspiracy with the legislature, they would pronounce the resolutions of such a majority contrary to the supreme law of the land, unconstitutional, and void. If the people were not tainted with the spirit of their State representatives, they, as the natural guardians of the Constitution, would throw their weight into the national scale and give it a decided preponderance in the contest. Attempts of this kind would not often be made lightly or rashly, because they could seldom be made without danger to their authors, except in cases of a tyrannical exercise of the federal authority.

If opposition to the national government should arise from the disorderly conduct of refractory or seditious individuals, it could be overcome by the same means that are daily used against the same evil under the State governments. The civil authorities, being equally ministers of the law of the land from whatever source it might come, would doubtless be as ready to guard the national regulations as the local ones against the inroads of private license. Consider those partial commotions and insurrections that sometimes disturb society, arising from the intrigues of an inconsiderable faction or from sudden or occasional ill humors that do not infect the great body of the community. For suppressing disturbances of that kind the general government could command more extensive resources than any single member could. As to those mortal feuds which, at certain junctures, spread a conflagration through a whole nation or through a very large part of it, whether they proceed from weighty causes of discontent given by the government or from the contagion of some violent popular fit, they do not fall within any ordinary rules of calculation. When they happen, they commonly amount to revolutions and dismemberments of empire. No form of government can always either avoid or control them. It is in vain to hope to guard against events too mighty for human foresight or precaution, and it would be idle to object to a government because it could not perform impossibilities.
